'''Sergei Mikhailovitch Voronin''' ({{langx|ru|Сергей Михайлович Воронин}}; March 11, 1946{{spaced ndash}}October 18, 1997)<ref name=obit/> was a Russian mathematician who specialized in [[number theory]]. He is known for a theorem showing that the critical strip of the [[Riemann zeta function]] has the property of [[Riemann_zeta_function#Universality|universality]].<ref name=vipschool/>

He also did work in [[additive number theory]] and applications of number theory to [[numerical analysis]].<ref name=additive/> He was also interested in the history of mathematics.

== Early life and education ==
Voronin's father was a petroleum engineer and his mother a teacher. He grew up in [[Buguruslan]] in the [[Orenburg]] region. He studied piano at a music school, successfully participated in mathematics competitions as a student and attended mathematics summer schools in Moscow. In 1963 he transferred to a special boarding school for mathematics in Moscow. In 1964 he entered [[Lomonosov University]], where he studied [[analytic number theory]] under [[Anatoly Karatsuba]]. In 1972, he received his PhD with the dissertation ''The Study of the Behavior of the Riemann Zeta Function'' under advisor Advisor [[Yulij Ilyashenko]].<ref name=geneal>[https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=87931  Yuli Ilyashenko at the Mathematics Genealogy Project]</ref> 

During the 1990s Voronin was a professor of number theory at the [[Moscow State Pedagogical University]].

== Career ==
In his dissertation, Voronin proved that the Riemann zeta function does not obey a continuous differential equation.<ref name=wolfram/> In 1975, as part of his habilitation thesis, he proved his universality theorem that any continuous non-vanishing analytic function in a circular disc can be approximated by the Riemann zeta function within the critical strip <math>\tfrac {1}{2}< \mathrm{Re} \, s < 1</math>.<ref name=voronin/>

The theorem shows the chaotic behavior of the Riemann zeta function in the critical strip. He also dealt with the distribution of zeros of other zeta functions (Dirichlet, Epstein).<ref name=dirichlet/> For example, in 1980 he showed that certain functions (in this case the Davenport-Heilbronn function, soon followed by some [[Epstein zeta function]]s)<ref name=davenport/> that are defined in the right half-plane by a [[Dirichlet series]] and satisfy a functional equation like the Riemann zeta function, but for which the Riemann hypothesis does not hold, nevertheless have an abnormal accumulation of zeros on the critical line.

== Voronin's universality theorem ==
Let <math>f</math> be a continuous function that has no zeros and is analytic inside the circular disc <math>D(r)</math> with <math>0 <r < \tfrac {1}{4}</math>. Then, for every real number <math>\epsilon > 0</math>, there exists a real number <math>\tau > 0</math> such that, for <math>| s | \leq r</math>
:<math>| \zeta (s + \tfrac {3}{4} + i \tau) - f (s) | < \epsilon</math>.

The theorem also holds for general [[Dirichlet L-function]]s. The theorem can also be formulated such that continuous, non-vanishing and analytic functions <math>f</math> in circular disks <math>D</math>, which lie in the strip <math>\tfrac{1}{2} < \mathrm{Re} \, s < 1</math>, can be approximated uniformly with arbitrary precision in <math>D</math> by translations of the Riemann zeta function along the imaginary axis <math>\zeta (s + i \tau)</math>. For example, Bhaskar Bagchi generalized it from circular disks to domains <math>D</math> that are simply connected and compact and lie in the strip <math>\tfrac{1}{2} < \mathrm{Re} \, s < 1</math>.<ref name=bagchi2/>

The [[Riemann hypothesis]] is equivalent to the theorem that the Riemann zeta function itself can also be approximated uniformly in the sense of Voronin's universality theorem.<ref name=bagchi/>
